title: Symmetry in nature and art: why so many shapes have matching parts

summary.text: Fold a hibiscus flower's picture down the middle, and the two halves match. Turn a snowflake one-sixth of the way round, and it looks the same again. Both are kinds of symmetry: a shape has symmetry when a part of it is repeated by flipping or turning. In this unit you blow a raft of soap bubbles and find that, in the middle, most of them press into six-sided shapes that nobody drew. At the edge, where the push is not the same on every side, the bubbles come out lopsided. The same idea helps explain snowflakes, flowers, honeycomb and the kolams and rangolis people draw. You also find out why a flower's even shape helps her bees, why animals that walk or swim have a left and a right side, and why no living body is perfectly even.
summary.art: A notebook page with a kolam drawn in white on one side, a six-armed snowflake in the middle and a five-petalled periwinkle flower on the other side, with dotted lines showing their lines of symmetry. Below, a plate of soap bubbles squashed into six-sided cells.

intro.hook: Look at a five-petalled flower, such as a periwinkle or a hibiscus. Now look at a kolam at a doorstep, or a rangoli at Diwali. A person drew the kolam carefully, turning it as she went. But who drew the flower? Nobody did. So how did the flower come out so even?
intro.text: People have asked this for a very long time. In this unit you look for two kinds of symmetry: shapes that match when folded, and shapes that match when turned. Then you make even shapes appear with soap bubbles, without drawing them. That gives you a real answer to how nature makes symmetry without a plan, and why the evenness sometimes breaks.
intro.art: A child's hand pointing from a white rice-flour kolam at a flat's doorstep to a pot of pink periwinkle flowers beside it, each flower with five matching petals.

outcomes: I can find a line of symmetry by folding a shape, and say whether a shape has no line, one line or many lines of symmetry.
I can find rotational symmetry by turning a shape, and count how many times it looks the same in one full turn (its order).
I can explain why bubbles pressed together in a raft come out six-sided in the middle and lopsided at the edge, using what I saw.
I can explain why a snowflake has six matching arms: the way water molecules join in ice, and all six arms growing in the same air.
I can say how a flower's symmetry helps her bees find her and land on her, and why animals that move forward have a left side and a right side.
I can draw a kolam or rangoli that has line symmetry and rotational symmetry, and point out both.
I can spot where symmetry breaks, such as at the edge of the bubble raft or in a plant beside a window, and say what was different on one side.

terms.meaning: A shape has symmetry when one part of it is repeated by flipping it or turning it, so the shape still looks the same.
terms.example: A steel thali looks the same however far you turn it. A butterfly's left wing matches the right wing.
terms.art: A round steel thali and a butterfly side by side, each with a dotted line or curved arrow showing how it matches itself.

terms.meaning: A line that cuts a shape into two halves that match exactly when you fold along it. It is also called a mirror line.
terms.example: Fold a paper heart down the middle, and the two halves sit exactly on top of each other. The fold is its line of symmetry.
terms.art: A paper heart folded in half, with the fold drawn as a dotted line.

terms.meaning: A shape has line symmetry when it has at least one line of symmetry. Some shapes have many lines.
terms.example: The letter A has one line of symmetry, down the middle. A square has four.
terms.art: The letter A with one dotted line, and a square with four dotted lines.

terms.meaning: A shape has rotational symmetry when you can turn it part of the way round its centre and it looks exactly the same as before.
terms.example: A ceiling fan with three blades looks the same after one-third of a turn.
terms.art: A three-bladed ceiling fan seen from below, with a curved arrow showing one-third of a turn.

terms.meaning: The number of times a shape looks exactly the same during one full turn. A shape that only matches itself at the end of a full turn has order 1, which means no rotational symmetry.
terms.example: A five-petalled periwinkle flower has order 5. The letter S has order 2.
terms.art: A periwinkle flower with its five petals numbered 1 to 5 and an arrow going once round.

terms.meaning: The point a shape turns around. In rotational symmetry, every repeated part is the same distance from the centre.
terms.example: The centre of a kolam is the dot in the middle. The arms of a snowflake all grow out from its centre.
terms.art: A kolam with a red dot at the centre and four matching loops around it.

terms.meaning: A flat shape with six straight sides.
terms.example: Each cell of a honeycomb is a hexagon. The squashed bubbles in the middle of a bubble raft are mostly hexagons too.
terms.art: A single hexagon next to a patch of honeycomb.

terms.meaning: The very thin skin of soapy water that makes the wall of a bubble. The film pulls itself as tight as it can, so its walls stay as short as possible.
terms.example: When you blow a bubble, the soap film pulls into a round ball, the shape with the least skin for the air inside.
terms.art: A soap bubble with arrows on its skin pointing inwards all round.

terms.meaning: The smallest bit of a substance that is still that substance. It is made of atoms joined together.
terms.example: A water molecule is made of one oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms. In ice, water molecules join up in rings of six.
terms.art: A drawing of water molecules as one big ball with two small balls, joined in a ring of six.

terms.meaning: An animal that carries pollen from one flower to another, so the plant can make seeds. Bees, butterflies, moths, some birds and bats are pollinators.
terms.example: A bee visits a sunflower for nectar, and yellow pollen sticks to her hairy body. She carries it to the next sunflower.
terms.art: A honeybee with yellow pollen on her legs, landing on a flower.

terms.meaning: Two-sided symmetry: a body or a flower with one line of symmetry, so it has a left half and a right half that match.
terms.example: Your body has bilateral symmetry. So does a tulsi flower, a pea flower and a butterfly.
terms.art: A child standing with arms out, with a dotted line from head to feet.

terms.meaning: Symmetry all the way round a centre, like the spokes of a wheel. The shape matches itself when turned, and it has several lines of symmetry.
terms.example: A hibiscus flower and a jellyfish have radial symmetry.
terms.art: A hibiscus flower seen from the front and a jellyfish seen from above, each with lines like wheel spokes.

terms.meaning: A pattern drawn on the ground at the doorstep, usually with rice flour, in Tamil Nadu and other parts of South India. A rangoli is a coloured floor pattern made in many parts of India, and has other names: alpona in Bengal, jhoti in Odisha and pookalam (made of flowers) in Kerala. Many kolams and rangolis are drawn with symmetry.
terms.example: A pulli kolam is drawn around a grid of dots. The line loops round the dots without touching them.
terms.art: A white pulli kolam of curved loops around a 3 by 3 grid of dots, at the door of a flat.

explanations.concept: Two kinds of symmetry: folding and turning
explanations.definition: A shape has line symmetry if you can fold it along a line so that the two halves match exactly. A shape has rotational symmetry if you can turn it part of the way round its centre and it looks exactly the same.
explanations.description: The fold test finds lines of symmetry. The turn test finds rotational symmetry. A shape can have one kind, both kinds, or neither. A butterfly has one line of symmetry but no rotational symmetry: turn it upside down and it looks different. The letter S has no line of symmetry, but it looks the same after half a turn. A five-petalled flower has both: five lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry. Your hand has neither.
examples: A butterfly: one line of symmetry, no rotational symmetry.
The letter S or the letter Z: no line of symmetry, but order 2 rotational symmetry.
A square kolam with four matching loops: four lines of symmetry and order 4.
Your hand: neither kind.
explanations.art: Four boxes: a butterfly with one dotted line, the letter S with a half-turn arrow, a square kolam with both, and a hand with a question mark.
explanations.context: This card explains the two kinds of symmetry you test in this unit: the fold test and the turn test.

explanations.definition: The order of rotational symmetry is the number of times a shape looks exactly the same during one full turn.
explanations.description: To count it, put a small mark on one corner of the shape, such as a bindi sticker. Turn the shape slowly round its centre. Count each time it looks exactly as it did at the start. Stop when the mark comes back to where it began. That count is the order. Every shape looks the same after one full turn, so a shape with order 1 has no rotational symmetry. A circle is special: it looks the same however little you turn it.
examples: A three-bladed ceiling fan: order 3.
A periwinkle flower with five petals: order 5.
A snowflake: order 6.
A star fruit cut across: order 5.
explanations.art: A paper star with a bindi on one point, shown five times as it turns, with the numbers 1 to 5.
explanations.context: This card shows how to count rotational symmetry. You need it for the turn test and the fruit experiment.

explanations.concept: Why bubbles in a raft become six-sided
explanations.definition: A soap film pulls itself as tight as it can. When bubbles of the same size crowd together, their walls meet three at a time, at equal angles. Each bubble in the middle is pressed equally by about six neighbours, so it becomes a six-sided cell.
explanations.description: A single bubble floating in the air is round. A ball is the shape that holds the air inside with the least skin. When many bubbles touch, each wall is shared by two bubbles, and the films pull the walls short and flat. Where walls meet, they always meet in threes, never in fours. A Belgian scientist, Joseph Plateau, wrote this rule down in 1873, after years of studying soap films. Three walls that pull equally settle at equal angles, a third of a full turn apart. When every bubble is the same size and is pressed equally on every side, the shape that fits these rules is a hexagon. At the edge of the raft, a bubble has neighbours on one side and open water or the plate on the other. The pushes are not even, so the bubble is lopsided. A bubble much smaller than its neighbours usually has fewer than six walls, and a bigger one usually has more.
examples: In the middle of a bubble raft, most bubbles have six walls.
At the edge, bubbles have a curved side and fewer walls.
Foam on a cup of filter coffee or in a sink of washing-up has the same three-wall meeting points.
explanations.art: A plate of squashed bubbles seen from above: neat hexagons in the middle, lopsided cells at the edge, and one meeting point circled to show three walls.
explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the bubble raft experiment. Do the experiment first, then read this.

explanations.concept: Why a snowflake has six matching arms
explanations.definition: A snowflake is a crystal of ice. In ice, water molecules join up in rings of six, so ice crystals grow in six directions. The six arms match because they all grow at the same time in the same air.
explanations.description: A snowflake starts as a tiny six-sided piece of ice high in a cloud. Water vapour, which is water as a gas, freezes onto its corners, and six arms grow out. As the snowflake falls, the air around it changes: a little warmer, a little colder, a little wetter, a little drier. Each change reaches all six arms at the same moment, because the snowflake is tiny. So when one arm grows a side branch, the other five grow the same branch. That is why the arms match with no plan. Each snowflake falls through slightly different air, so big branching snowflakes almost never look exactly the same. Most real snowflakes are also a little uneven, because they bump or because one side meets slightly different air. The scientist Ukichiro Nakaya grew snowflakes in a cold laboratory in Japan in the 1930s. He showed that the temperature and the moisture of the air decide whether a snowflake grows as flat plates, long needles or branching stars.
examples: A snowflake has six arms, never eight. Paper snowflakes folded into eight make eight arms, which real ones never grow.
Frost on a cold window can grow in feathery branches for the same reason.
Snow falls in winter in Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh.
explanations.art: One snowflake falling through bands of air drawn in different colours, with all six arms growing the same branch at the same band.
explanations.context: This card explains why a snowflake has six matching arms. In most of India, you will meet snowflakes only in pictures or in the hills.

explanations.description: A plant cannot walk to another plant to share her pollen. She needs a pollinator, such as a bee, to visit and carry the pollen for her. Her flowers have to be easy for a bee to find, and to land on the right way. Many flowers solve this with symmetry. A flower's parts grow in rings around the tip of the bud, so petals often come in fives, as in hibiscus and periwinkle, or in sixes, in two rings of three, as in lilies and onion flowers. These round flowers can be visited from any side. Other flowers, such as tulsi, peas and orchids, have one line of symmetry. They have a lip at the bottom where a bee lands, always the same way up. Then the pollen touches the same place on every bee's body, and is carried to the same place in the next flower. Experiments show that honeybees can learn to tell symmetrical patterns from lopsided ones, and that many bees prefer symmetrical ones. Scientists are still finding out how much this preference shaped flowers.
examples: Hibiscus and periwinkle: five petals in a ring.
Tulsi and pea flowers: one line of symmetry, with a landing lip.
A sunflower head is made of hundreds of tiny flowers packed in spirals around the centre.

perspectives.explanation: Symmetry mostly comes from how a bud grows: parts form in rings around the tip, so they come out evenly spaced. The bees then pick the plants whose flowers suit them.

In experiments, honeybees learned symmetrical patterns and often preferred them. Bees choosing symmetrical flowers may have helped make flowers more symmetrical over a very long time. How strong this effect is, is still being studied.

explanations.art: A bee landing on the lower lip of a tulsi flower, next to a round hibiscus flower with a bee coming in from the side.
explanations.context: This card is about why flowers have even shapes. It starts with the plant's own problem: she needs bees to visit.

explanations.concept: Why animals that move have a left side and a right side
explanations.definition: Animals that move forward through the world, such as people, fish, birds, ants and earthworms, have bilateral symmetry: a left half and a right half that nearly match. Animals that stay in one place or drift, such as jellyfish and sea anemones, often have radial symmetry.
explanations.description: An animal that moves forward meets the world front first. The front is where her mouth and eyes are, because that is where food and danger come from. Her left side and right side meet the world in the same way, so they nearly match. A jellyfish drifts in the sea, and food and danger can come from any side. So her body is the same all the way round. A starfish is a surprise. Her young, called larvae, are tiny and two-sided, and they swim. Only later do they grow into a five-armed shape.
examples: You: two eyes, two ears, two arms and two legs, one on each side.
A fish: fins on the left and right, mouth at the front.
A jellyfish: the same all the way round.
explanations.art: A fish swimming forward with a dotted line along her middle, and a jellyfish from above with spoke lines.
explanations.context: This card explains why most animals have a left and a right side that match.

explanations.concept: Nothing in nature is perfectly even
explanations.definition: Real living bodies and natural shapes are nearly symmetrical, never exactly. Their symmetry breaks wherever one side meets something different.
explanations.description: Your heart sits a little to the left of your chest. Most people's two feet are slightly different sizes. A plant on a windowsill grows more leaves on the side facing the light, and bends towards it. In the bubble raft, the bubbles at the edge are lopsided because they are pressed on one side only. A snowflake that meets warmer air on one side grows uneven arms. Each break in symmetry is a clue: it tells you that one side met something the other side did not.
examples: A money plant on a windowsill leans towards the window.
A tree at the edge of a road grows more branches on the open side.
Your two hand spans are close, but measure them, and they are often a little different.
explanations.art: A potted plant on a windowsill leaning towards the window, with more leaves on the light side.
explanations.context: This card is about where symmetry breaks, and what that tells you.

explanations.definition: People make symmetrical art by repeating one part: they draw it, then flip it or turn it and draw it again.
explanations.description: To draw a pulli kolam, you first put down a grid of dots. Then you loop a line around the dots. Many kolam artists draw one quarter, then turn and draw the same loops on the next quarter, until they have gone all the way round. That gives order 4 rotational symmetry. If the loops in each quarter are themselves mirror images, the kolam also has lines of symmetry. Rangolis, the alpona of Bengal, the jhoti of Odisha, the pookalam of Kerala, mandalas, temple floor tiles and the patterns on a Kanchipuram saree border use the same tricks of flipping and turning. Mathematicians, such as Gift Siromoney in Chennai in the 1970s, have studied the rules inside kolams.
examples: A pulli kolam drawn round a 3 by 3 grid of dots.
A rangoli with eight matching petals at Diwali.
A tiled floor where one tile, turned and repeated, makes the whole pattern.
explanations.art: Four stages of a kolam being drawn: dots, one quarter, two quarters, all four quarters.
explanations.context: This card shows how people make symmetrical art by flipping and turning one part.

agreed.text: In ice, water molecules join in rings of six. This is why snowflakes and other ice crystals grow with six-fold symmetry.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have shone X-rays through ice and measured exactly where the molecules sit. Photographs of snowflakes, starting with Wilson Bentley's in 1885, show six arms.

agreed.text: Where soap films meet, they meet three at a time, at equal angles.
agreed.evidence: Joseph Plateau set out these rules in 1873. Anyone can check them in a raft of bubbles, and they have been confirmed by many experiments and by mathematics.

agreed.text: Most animals that move forward have bilateral symmetry, a left side and a right side.
agreed.evidence: This is true of almost every animal group, from earthworms and ants to fish, birds and people.

agreed.text: Honeycomb cells are hexagons, which cover a flat space with no gaps and use the least wall for the space they hold.
agreed.evidence: That hexagons do this best was guessed long ago and finally proved by the mathematician Thomas Hales in 1999.

agreed.text: No living body is perfectly symmetrical.
agreed.evidence: Measure any body carefully and the two sides differ a little. In people, the heart sits to the left and most organs are not in matching pairs.

challenging.claim: Symmetry in nature needs a designer who plans it, like a person drawing a kolam.
challenging.who: A common idea, and the view of some older writers
challenging.for: Symmetrical things look planned, and the symmetrical things people make are planned.
challenging.against: Bubbles, snowflakes and crystals become symmetrical with no plan drawn, because the same rules act equally on every side. You can watch it happen in the bubble raft.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that an even shape must have been planned by someone.

challenging.who: A common idea, from neat pictures and paper cut-outs
challenging.for: Photographs of snowflakes chosen for books show beautiful matching arms.
challenging.against: Photographers pick the best ones. Most real snowflakes are a little uneven, broken, or stuck to others. Snow scientists such as Kenneth Libbrecht say this plainly.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that every snowflake is perfectly even.

challenging.for: A snowflake's shape depends on the exact air it falls through, and each falls a slightly different way. So big branching snowflakes are almost certain to differ.
challenging.against: Very small, simple snow crystals, such as plain six-sided plates, can look the same. Scientists have grown near-identical twin snowflakes side by side in the laboratory.
challenging.context: This card is about the saying that no two snowflakes are alike. It is mostly true, but not completely.

challenging.claim: People find symmetrical faces more beautiful because symmetry is a sign of health.
challenging.for: In some studies, people rate more symmetrical faces as more attractive.
challenging.against: Other studies find the link to health is weak or missing. People may simply find symmetrical shapes easier to see and remember.
challenging.context: This card is about a debate: why many people like symmetrical faces and shapes.

big_questions.q: In the bubble raft, the bubbles in the middle became six-sided, and nobody drew them. What else around you might have an even shape with no plan behind it?
big_questions.hint: Think of foam, cracks in dry mud, drops on a window, the rings when a stone drops in water.

big_questions.q: A snowflake's six arms grow in the same air at the same time. Do two leaves on the same branch grow in the same conditions? Do they match?
big_questions.hint: Pick two leaves from opposite sides of one stem and compare them.

big_questions.q: Your left hand and right hand are mirror images. Can you ever turn your left glove so it fits your right hand?
big_questions.hint: Try it with a glove or a sock with a heel. What about turning it inside out?

big_questions.q: Why do so many people, all over the world, make symmetrical art, from kolams to mandalas to carpets?
big_questions.hint: Is it because nature shows us symmetry, because it is easier to draw, or because our eyes like it?

big_questions.q: Is a little unevenness a mistake, or is it what makes each living thing different from every other?
big_questions.hint: Look at your own face in a photo, then at the same photo made with two left halves. Which looks like you?

story.title: The Kolam by the Shoe Rack
story.note: Made-up story. Kolams drawn at doorsteps in the month of Margazhi, soap walls meeting three at a time, and plants leaning to the light are all real.
text: Meenakshi lived on the fourth floor of a block of flats in Chennai. Every morning in the month of Margazhi, she drew a kolam outside the door of flat 4B. Her paati had taught her when she was five. Now she was nine, and she could draw a kolam of twenty-five dots without stopping.
Her cousin Arjun had come from Pune for the holidays. He was seven. He sat on the steps in his pyjamas and watched her put down the dots, five rows of five.
"Why do you turn round and round?" he asked.
"I draw one corner," said Meenakshi, "then I turn, and draw the same thing on the next corner. Four corners, four turns. That way all four sides match."
"So you make it even on purpose," said Arjun. "Nature doesn't do that. Nature is messy. Only people make things even."
Meenakshi stopped with the rice flour between her fingers. She looked at the pot of periwinkle by the lift. Every pink flower had five petals, spaced out evenly round a little dark eye.
"Who turned round and round to draw those?" she asked.
Arjun shrugged. "The plant, I suppose."
"The plant can't hold rice flour," said Meenakshi. "But she gets five even petals every time."

There was one problem with the kolam outside 4B. The neighbours' big shoe rack stood right beside the door. Every morning, the corner of the kolam next to the shoe rack came out squashed. There wasn't enough room for the loop. The other three corners were round and full. That one was flat and pinched.
"Your kolam isn't even," said Arjun, pointing.
"That's the shoe rack's fault," said Meenakshi.

That afternoon, it was Meenakshi's turn to wash the steel plates after lunch. The sink filled up with soapy water. A raft of little bubbles gathered in one big steel plate, all squeezed together. She bent down to look.
The bubbles were not round. They had straight walls. In the middle of the plate, nearly every bubble had six walls, like the cells of a honeycomb.
"Arjun! Come here!"
He came, dripping, from the bathroom. "What?"
"Who drew these?"
He looked. "Nobody. They're bubbles."
"But they're hexagons. Six sides. Count."
Arjun counted, poking each wall with a wet finger. "Six. Six. Six. Five. Six."
"Now look at the edge," said Meenakshi.

At the rim of the plate, the bubbles were different. Each one had bubbles on one side and the steel rim on the other. Their outer sides were curved, and they had only three or four walls. They were lopsided.
"The middle ones are even," said Arjun slowly. "The edge ones are squashed."
"Like my kolam by the shoe rack," said Meenakshi. "In the middle, every bubble has the same neighbours pushing on every side. So it comes out even. At the edge, something is in the way on one side."
"So nobody drew them," said Arjun. "They just got pushed the same way all round."
"Look where the walls meet," said Meenakshi. She pointed with a fork. "Three walls. Always three. Never four."
Arjun checked five places, then ten. Always three.

The next morning, they drew the kolam together. Arjun put down the dots. Meenakshi drew the first corner, and Arjun copied it on the next, turning round and round. When they reached the corner by the shoe rack, Arjun said, "Wait." He went inside and asked Paati if they could move the dots one step towards the stairs, away from the rack. Paati laughed and said yes.
This time, the four corners had the same room. The kolam came out even all the way round.
On the last day of his holiday, Arjun stood by the periwinkle pot. "Meenakshi," he said, "there's a plant on our balcony in Pune that leans towards the window. She has more leaves on that side."

"Then she gets more light on that side," said Meenakshi. "Something is different there, so she's not even. When everything is the same all round, things come out even. When one side is different, you can see it in the shape."
Arjun nodded. On the train home he drew a kolam in his notebook, one corner at a time, turning the book round and round.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the bubbles became six-sided because each one in the middle was pressed equally on every side by bubbles of the same size, and soap walls always meet three at a time at equal angles. Nobody drew the hexagons. At the edge, the push was not the same on every side, so the bubbles were lopsided, just as the kolam corner beside the shoe rack was squashed. A person makes a kolam even by turning and repeating. Bubbles, snowflakes and many growing things come out even when the same thing happens on every side. A flower's evenness also comes from how her bud grows, in rings round a centre. Where one side meets something different, like light from a window, the symmetry breaks, and the break tells you what was different.
ask: Arjun said only people make things even. What made him change his mind?
Why was the kolam corner by the shoe rack squashed? What was the same about the bubbles at the edge of the plate?
How did Meenakshi and Arjun fix the kolam?
Why does the plant in Pune have more leaves on one side?
Can you find something at home that is even in the middle but lopsided at its edge?

games.title: Turn Snap: match the order of symmetry
games.context: This is a card game. Each card names a shape from nature or art. Players snap when two cards have the same order of rotational symmetry.

rules: Shuffle the 24 cards and deal them out equally, face down. Keep your pile face down. The back of each card shows its order, so try not to peek. The back is there to check when players disagree about a snap.
Take turns to turn over your top card onto a pile in the middle.
If the new card has the same order of rotational symmetry as the card just below it, the first to say 'Snap!' and the order wins the middle pile. Put won cards face down beside you.
Say the order out loud, for example 'Snap, five!'. If you snap when the orders are different, or say the wrong number, the other player (or the player to your left) wins the pile.
If your pile runs out, you can still snap. The game ends when every card has been turned over, or after 10 minutes. The player with the most won cards wins; a tie is a shared win.
Playing alone: guess the order of each card, then turn it over to check the back. Sort the cards into piles by order. Time yourself, and try to beat your time.

flow.kid: Turn over a card. Same order as the one below? Shout snap and the number!
flow.parent: The order is written on the back of each card. A butterfly, a face, a tulsi flower and a leaf have order 1: they have a line of symmetry but no rotational symmetry. Draw a small picture on each card if you like.

flow.do: Look at the order 1 cards together.
flow.say: The butterfly, the face, the tulsi flower and the leaf have order 1, so they do not match when turned. Can you find a fold line on each one?
flow.kid: Look at the order 1 cards. Do they have a fold line?

check.q: A butterfly, a tulsi flower and your face all have order 1. What do they have in common?
options: They have no symmetry at all
They each have one line of symmetry, a left side and a right side
They all have six parts
check.why: They have bilateral symmetry: one line of symmetry, but no rotational symmetry. A butterfly and a face meet the world front first. A tulsi flower has a lip where bees land the same way up every time.

games.title: Finish My Half: a dot-grid partner game
games.context: This is a drawing game on a dot grid. One player draws half or one quarter of a pattern, and the other finishes it so that it has symmetry.

printables.title: 8 dot-grid sheets
items: Mirror sheet 1: a square of 8 by 8 dots with a dotted line of symmetry down the middle
Mirror sheet 2: a square of 8 by 8 dots with a dotted line of symmetry down the middle
Mirror sheet 3: a square of 8 by 8 dots with a dotted line of symmetry down the middle
Mirror sheet 4: a square of 8 by 8 dots with a dotted line of symmetry down the middle
Four-quarter sheet 1: a square of 8 by 8 dots with a cross through the middle, making four quarters
Four-quarter sheet 2: a square of 8 by 8 dots with a cross through the middle, making four quarters
Four-quarter sheet 3: a square of 8 by 8 dots with a cross through the middle, making four quarters
Four-quarter sheet 4: a square of 8 by 8 dots with a cross through the middle, making four quarters

rules: Play in pairs. With 4 players, make two pairs who play at the same time. No printer? Draw an 8 by 8 square of dots on squared paper and mark the dotted line or the cross yourself.
Mirror sheet: Player 1 draws 5 straight lines joining dots on one side of the dotted line only. Player 2 draws the mirror image on the other side, so the dotted line becomes a line of symmetry.
Check by folding the sheet along the dotted line and holding it up to a window: each new line should land exactly on a drawn line. Player 2 scores 1 point for each correct line.

Four-quarter sheet: Player 1 draws 3 lines in one quarter. Player 2 turns the sheet a quarter turn and copies them into the next quarter, and so on until all four quarters match. Player 2 scores 1 point for each correct quarter, up to 3.
Swap roles after each sheet. After 4 sheets (2 mirror, 2 four-quarter), the higher total wins; a tie is a shared win.
Playing alone: draw your half, cover it, then try to draw the other half from memory. Uncover it and check by folding. Score the same way.

setup.art: A dot grid with a dotted line down the middle and a few lines drawn on the left side only.
setup.caption: 1. One player draws on one side.

setup.art: The same grid with the matching mirror lines drawn on the right side.
setup.caption: 2. The other finishes the other half.

flow.do: Play two mirror sheets, one with each of you as the drawer.
flow.say: I'll draw 5 lines on my side. You draw the matching lines on your side, so the dotted line becomes a line of symmetry. Then we swap.
flow.kid: Your partner draws 5 lines on one side. Draw the matching lines on your side.
flow.context: This is round 1 of Finish My Half. You finish a drawing so it has a line of symmetry.

flow.do: Play two four-quarter sheets, one with each of you as the drawer.
flow.say: Now I'll draw 3 lines in one quarter. You turn the sheet a quarter turn and copy them, until all four quarters match. Then we swap.
flow.kid: Your partner draws in one quarter. Turn the paper. Copy it into each quarter.
flow.parent: Many children copy without turning, which gives a mirror image instead of a turned copy. Both are symmetry, but different kinds. Point out the difference.

flow.do: Compare a mirror sheet and a four-quarter sheet.
flow.say: Which sheet has a fold line? Which looks the same when turned? Can one have both?
flow.kid: Which pattern folds to match? Which turns to match?

check.q: In round 2, you copied one quarter by turning the sheet a quarter turn each time. What kind of symmetry does the finished pattern always have?
options: Rotational symmetry of order 4
Exactly one line of symmetry
No symmetry
check.why: Copying by turning gives a pattern that looks the same after each quarter turn, so it has order 4. It has lines of symmetry as well only if the lines in the first quarter were themselves mirror images.

experiments.title: The Bubble Raft: what shape do crowded bubbles take?
experiments.question: When many bubbles of the same size crowd together in one flat layer, what shape does each bubble take? Is it the same in the middle and at the edge?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Each bubble starts round. When they are squashed together under a lid, what shape will a bubble in the middle become: round, square, triangle, six-sided, or all different? Will the edge bubbles be the same as the middle ones? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Blow every bubble the same way, so they are all about the same size. Count the walls of 5 bubbles in the middle and 5 bubbles at the edge, because one bubble on its own could be odd. Count the same way each time: go round the bubble and point at each wall once with the toothpick.
results_table: Is it even all round? (yes or no)

materials.item: a steel plate with a rim, such as a thali or a deep plate
a clear plastic lid from a takeaway box, or a clear plastic file sheet, bigger than your palm
dishwashing liquid
water
sugar, to make the bubbles last longer (if you have it)
a drinking straw
a toothpick, for pointing at walls while counting
a torch or a bright window

experiments.safety: Blow out through the straw, never suck in. Soapy water stings the eyes.

schedule.what: Mix soapy water, blow a raft of bubbles, cover it with a clear lid and count the walls of bubbles in the middle and at the edge.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw 3 middle bubbles and 3 edge bubbles exactly as you see them. Mark one place where walls meet, and write how many walls meet there.

setup.art: A cup of water with dishwashing liquid being stirred gently with a spoon, and the soapy water poured into a steel plate.
setup.caption: 1. Mix the soapy water and pour it into the plate.

setup.art: A child blowing gently through a straw held just under the soapy water, with a patch of same-sized bubbles growing on the plate.
setup.caption: 2. Blow gently so the bubbles come out one at a time, all the same size.

setup.art: A clear plastic lid laid gently on top of the bubble patch, and the bubbles squashed into six-sided cells beneath it.
setup.caption: 3. Lay a clear lid on top. Count the walls of each bubble.

flow.do: 1. Pour 1 cup of water into a bowl. 2. Add 1 tablespoon of dishwashing liquid and 1 teaspoon of sugar. 3. Stir slowly, without making foam. 4. Pour it into the plate. The layer should be a few millimetres deep, enough to cover the tip of the straw.
flow.say: We are going to make a raft of bubbles. Stir gently, because we don't want foam yet. We want to make the bubbles ourselves, one at a time.
flow.kid: Mix water, dishwash liquid and sugar in a bowl. Stir slowly. Pour it into the plate.
flow.parent: A layer 5 mm to 1 cm deep works best, just deep enough for the straw's tip to sit under the surface. If the tip does not go under, add more soapy water. Sugar helps the bubbles last longer, but the test works without it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the bubble raft experiment. Here you make the soapy water.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess and give a reason. Write the guess at the top of the record sheet.
flow.say: Each bubble starts round. When we squash lots of them together under a lid, what shape will a bubble in the middle become? What about one at the edge? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Each bubble starts round. What shape will it be when squashed? Will edge bubbles look the same? Write your guess and why.

ask.q: What shape do you think the middle bubbles will be, and why?
good: Any guess with a reason. For example: squares, because they fit together like tiles. Or round, because bubbles are always round.

flow.parent: Don't give the answer. Any guess with a reason is a good start. The test will answer it.

flow.do: 1. Hold the straw so its tip is just under the surface of the soapy layer. 2. Blow very gently, so bubbles come out one at a time, each about the size of a green pea. 3. Move the tip a little each time, so the bubbles crowd together in one layer. 4. Make a patch at least as big as your palm. 5. If a bubble climbs on top of others, pop it with a dry fingertip.
flow.say: Blow as gently as you can. Small, same-sized bubbles are what we want. Keep them in one flat layer, side by side.
flow.kid: Put the straw tip just under the soapy water. Blow very gently. Make lots of small bubbles, all the same size. Keep them side by side in one layer.
flow.parent: Blowing too hard makes big bubbles of mixed sizes. That still works, but the pattern is harder to see. If the bubbles keep popping, add another teaspoon of dishwashing liquid. Bubbles last longest away from a fan.

flow.do: 1. Hold the clear lid flat above the bubble patch. 2. Lower it gently until it rests on the bubbles. 3. Shine the torch from the side, low across the plate, or put the plate by a bright window. 4. Look down through the lid.
flow.say: Now we squash them gently. The lid presses every bubble down to the same height. Let's look from above. What shape are they now?
flow.kid: Lay the clear lid gently on the bubbles. Shine the torch from the side. Look down through the lid. What shapes do you see?

ask.q: What do you notice about the shapes?
good: The bubbles have straight walls now.
They fit together with no gaps.
The middle ones look six-sided.

flow.parent: The walls show up best with light coming low from one side. These bubbles are low domes, not flat cells, so expect most middle bubbles to look six-sided, with some five- or seven-sided, and a few round ones if the sizes are mixed. No clear lid? Look at the raft without one. Count how many bubbles touch each middle bubble. Most touch six.

flow.do: 1. Choose 5 bubbles in the middle. 2. For each one, point at each wall once with the toothpick, held just above the lid, and count. 3. Choose 5 bubbles at the edge, and count their walls too. 4. Write each count in the table.
flow.say: Let's count, not just look. Point at each wall once with the toothpick as you go round. Then do the same at the edge.
flow.kid: Pick 5 middle bubbles. Count the walls of each one. Then pick 5 edge bubbles. Count again. Write the numbers down.
flow.parent: Expect most middle bubbles to have 6 walls. A few may have 5 or 7, usually because they are a different size: smaller bubbles tend to have fewer walls, bigger ones more. Edge bubbles have a curved side facing open water or the plate, and fewer walls.

flow.do: Ask your child to find three places where walls meet, and count the walls at each one.
flow.say: Look where the walls join. How many walls meet at each joining point? Check three different places.
flow.kid: Find a place where walls join. How many walls meet there? Check two more places.

check.q: In the bubble raft, how many soap walls meet at each joining point?
options: It is different every time
check.why: Soap walls always meet three at a time, at equal angles. Joseph Plateau wrote this rule down in 1873. If you thought 4, look again closely: four walls sometimes seem to meet for a moment, but they quickly slide apart into two meetings of three.

flow.parent: Three walls meeting at equal angles is the key fact. It is why the middle cells become six-sided.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why. Write it under the table.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see that tells you? Why do you think the middle bubbles and the edge bubbles are different?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think now, what you saw, and why you think the middle bubbles and the edge bubbles are different.

ask.q: Why were the middle bubbles six-sided, but the edge bubbles lopsided?
good: The middle bubbles were pressed equally from every side by their neighbours.
The edge bubbles had bubbles on one side and nothing on the other side.
The push was the same all round in the middle, but not at the edge.

check.q: Nobody drew the hexagons in the bubble raft. What made them?
options: The lid has hexagons printed on it
Each middle bubble was pressed equally on every side by bubbles of the same size
Soap is made of tiny hexagons
The sugar
check.why: Every middle bubble had neighbours of the same size pressing equally from every side, and soap walls pull themselves short. The even push all round gave an even, six-sided shape. At the edge the push was not the same on every side, so the shape was lopsided. Soap itself is not six-sided, and the lid is plain.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses the edge bubbles as evidence: same soap, same lid, same size, but a different push around them, and a different shape.

experiments.title: Cut Across and Count: do fruits repeat their pattern?
experiments.question: When you cut a fruit across its middle, the inside often repeats around the centre. How many times does it repeat? Is that number the same in every fruit of one kind?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will two bhindis cut across show the same number of seed rows? Will two lemons show the same number of segments? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Cut every fruit across its widest middle, never along its length, so you compare the same view. Cut 2 of each kind, because one fruit could be unusual. Count each one twice.
results_table: Fruit 1: how many parts around the centre?

materials.item: bhindi (lady's finger)
lemons
cucumbers
a tomato
any 2 more fruits or vegetables you have: an apple, a banana, a capsicum, a mosambi (sweet lime), an orange, a star fruit, a guava
a knife and a chopping board, used by a grown-up

experiments.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting. Lemon juice stings cuts and eyes.

schedule.what: Cut fruits across their middles, count the repeating parts around the centre, and compare two fruits of each kind.

experiments.record: Draw each cut face from above, with the centre marked. Fill in the table.

setup.art: A grown-up's hands cutting a bhindi straight across its middle on a wooden board, with a lemon and a cucumber waiting.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts each fruit across its middle.

setup.art: The cut face of a bhindi showing five seed rows in a ring, with a finger pointing and counting.
setup.caption: 2. Count the parts around the centre.

setup.art: A notebook table with drawings of a bhindi, lemon and cucumber cut across, and numbers written beside each.
setup.caption: 3. Draw each one and write the number.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the fruits. 2. Ask your child to guess, for each kind, how many parts will repeat around the centre. 3. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: When we cut these across, the inside will have a pattern around the middle. How many times will it repeat in a bhindi? In a lemon? Will two of the same kind match? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at each fruit. Guess how many parts are inside, around the middle. Will two lemons match? Write your guesses and why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the fruit experiment. You guess, then cut fruits across and count the repeating parts inside.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts each fruit straight across its widest middle. 2. Lay each piece cut side up on the board. 3. Wipe the cut faces with a cloth if they are too wet to see.
flow.say: I'll cut, and you watch. Look at the cut face. Can you find the centre?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut each fruit across the middle. Look at each cut face. Find the centre.
flow.parent: Always cut across, like slicing a cucumber for salad, never along the length. Cook or eat the cut fruit afterwards, so nothing is wasted.

flow.do: 1. For each cut face, count the parts arranged around the centre. In a bhindi, count seed rows. In a lemon, count segments. In a tomato, cucumber or capsicum, count seed rooms. 2. Count twice. 3. Write both fruits of each kind in the table.
flow.say: Count the parts around the middle. Touch each one as you count. Then count again to be sure.
flow.kid: Count the parts around the middle. Touch each one. Count again. Write the number.
flow.parent: Most bhindis show 5 seed rows, though some kinds have more. A cucumber usually shows 3 seed parts. An apple usually shows a five-pointed star of seed rooms. A banana shows a faint three-part pattern. Lemons often differ: one may have 8 segments and the other 10 or 11. Tomatoes differ a lot too, from 2 rooms to many. Whatever you find is the real answer.

flow.do: Compare your numbers. Which kinds matched, and which did not? Then answer the question below.
flow.say: Which fruits gave the same number both times? Which ones changed?
flow.kid: Which fruits matched both times? Which ones did not?

check.q: Two bhindis and two lemons are cut across. Both bhindis have 5 seed rows. One lemon has 9 segments and the other has 11. What does this show?
options: The lemons were cut wrongly
Some kinds of fruit keep the same number of parts, and others vary
Lemons have no rotational symmetry at all
Bhindi is not a fruit
check.why: The number of parts in a fruit is set by the flower it grew from. Each part grew from one part of the flower's centre. Bhindi flowers are very regular, so bhindis of one kind usually show the same number every time. Lemon flowers vary more, so lemons do too. Both lemons still have rotational symmetry, just a different order.

flow.parent: The parts inside a fruit grew from the flower's centre, one part for each section. Each section holds and feeds a row of seeds.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: What do you think now about fruits and symmetry? What did you see? Why might a lemon vary but a bhindi not?
flow.kid: Say what you think now about fruits and symmetry, what you saw, and why a lemon might vary but a bhindi not.

ask.q: Why might every bhindi have 5 seed rows?
good: Because bhindi flowers grow 5 parts in their centre.
Because each row grew from one part of the flower.

activities.title: Fold or Turn? A home symmetry hunt

materials.item: 8 flat things from home: a steel plate, a leaf, a flower, a biscuit, a coin, a spoon, a picture of a butterfly, a bangle
a bindi sticker or a small piece of paper
a piece of thread as long as your arm

schedule.what: Test 8 things from home with the fold test and the turn test.

activities.record: Make two columns: 'Folds to match' and 'Turns to match'. Write each thing in one column, both, or neither.

setup.art: A thread laid straight across a leaf on a table, showing two matching halves.
setup.caption: 1. The fold test: lay a thread across. Do the halves match?

setup.art: A steel plate with a bindi on its rim, being turned slowly by a child's hands.
setup.caption: 2. The turn test: stick a bindi on one edge and turn slowly.

flow.do: Gather 8 flat things and put them on a table.
flow.say: Let's go on a symmetry hunt. Bring me 8 flat things from the house.
flow.kid: Find 8 flat things at home. Put them on the table.
flow.context: This is a quick hunt at the start of the unit. You test everyday things to see if they match when folded or turned.

flow.do: 1. For each thing, lay the thread across it in a straight line. 2. Ask: would the two halves match if you folded it along the thread? 3. Try several directions.
flow.say: Think of folding it along the thread. Would one half sit exactly on the other? Try the thread a different way too.
flow.kid: Lay the thread across. Would the two halves match if folded? Try other ways too.

ask.q: Which things have a line of symmetry?
good: The leaf, down its middle vein.
The butterfly.
The plate, in many directions.

flow.do: 1. Stick the bindi on the edge of one thing. 2. Turn it slowly on the table. 3. Count each time it looks exactly as it did at the start, until the bindi is back where it began.
flow.say: Now the turn test. Turn it slowly. Every time it looks exactly the same, count one.
flow.kid: Stick the bindi on one edge. Turn it slowly. Count each time it looks the same.

check.q: You turn a leaf all the way round. It only looks the same when the bindi comes back to the start. What does that mean?
options: The leaf has no rotational symmetry
The leaf has order 4
The leaf has no line of symmetry
check.why: Everything looks the same after a full turn. A thing that matches only then has order 1, which means no rotational symmetry. The leaf may still have a line of symmetry down its middle vein.

flow.do: Ask which thing surprised your child most.
flow.say: Which one surprised you? Did anything have both kinds of symmetry?
flow.kid: Which one surprised you? Did anything have both kinds of symmetry?

activities.title: Draw a Pulli Kolam with four matching quarters

materials.item: rice flour or chalk, for a doorstep or balcony floor, or a pencil and paper

schedule.what: Draw a 3 by 3 dot kolam, one quarter at a time, then find its symmetry.

activities.record: Draw or photograph your kolam. Draw its lines of symmetry in pencil and write its order of rotational symmetry.

setup.art: A 3 by 3 grid of rice-flour dots on a floor tile.
setup.caption: 1. Put down 9 dots in 3 rows of 3.

setup.art: One loop drawn around the dots in the top-left quarter, with an arrow showing the paper being turned a quarter turn.
setup.caption: 2. Draw one quarter, then turn and repeat.

setup.art: The finished kolam with four matching quarters and dotted lines of symmetry.
setup.caption: 3. Finish all four quarters and find the lines of symmetry.

flow.do: Put down 9 dots in 3 rows of 3, evenly spaced, about two fingers apart.
flow.say: A pulli kolam starts with dots. Women in Tamil Nadu draw these at the doorstep every morning, often without lifting their hand.
flow.kid: Put down 9 dots. Make 3 rows of 3. Keep them evenly spaced.
flow.context: This activity is about drawing a kolam, a South Indian doorstep pattern, and finding its symmetry.

flow.do: 1. Draw a curved line looping round the corner dot of one quarter, without touching any dot. 2. Turn the paper a quarter turn, or walk a quarter of the way round the kolam. 3. Draw the same loop again. 4. Repeat until all four quarters are done.
flow.say: Draw one loop round the corner dot. Now turn, and draw exactly the same loop. Turning and repeating is what makes the kolam even.
flow.kid: Loop a line round one corner dot. Don't touch the dot. Turn the paper. Draw the same loop. Do all four corners.
flow.parent: It doesn't need to be perfect. Wobbly kolams still show the idea: the pattern repeats each quarter turn. If you draw with rice flour indoors, sweep it up afterwards.

flow.do: 1. Ask how many times the kolam looks the same in one full turn. 2. Look for lines of symmetry. Lay a thread across.
flow.say: Turn it slowly in your mind, or turn the paper. How many times does it look the same? Now find a fold line.
flow.kid: How many times does your kolam look the same in one turn? Find its fold lines too.

check.q: A kolam is drawn by repeating one quarter, turning a quarter turn each time. What is its order of rotational symmetry?
check.why: One quarter repeated four times matches itself after each quarter turn, so it looks the same 4 times in one full turn. If the loops in each quarter are mirror images too, the kolam also has lines of symmetry.

flow.do: Ask your child to change one quarter on purpose, then look again.
flow.say: Now change one quarter: add an extra loop there only. What happens to the symmetry?
flow.kid: Add an extra loop to one corner only. Does it still match when turned?

ask.q: What happened when you changed one quarter only?
good: It doesn't look the same when turned any more.
The symmetry broke on that side.

activities.title: A Real Snowflake Has Six Arms: fold and cut one

materials.item: a square of thin paper, such as a newspaper page cut square
scissors

activities.safety: Children under 8 cut with a grown-up beside them. Cut away from your fingers.

schedule.what: Fold paper into six and cut a snowflake with six matching arms.

activities.record: Stick your snowflake in your notebook. Write its order of rotational symmetry and how many lines of symmetry it has.

setup.art: A square paper folded into a triangle, then the triangle folded into three equal parts like a fan.
setup.caption: 1. Fold the square into a triangle, then into three.

setup.art: The folded wedge with small notches cut along both edges.
setup.caption: 2. Cut small shapes from both edges.

setup.art: The opened paper snowflake with six matching arms.
setup.caption: 3. Open it. Count the arms.

flow.do: 1. Fold the square corner to corner into a triangle. 2. Fold it in half again into a smaller triangle. 3. Fold this into three equal parts, like a fan, one part over the front and one behind. 4. Cut off the uneven top straight across.
flow.say: Most paper snowflakes are folded into eight, but a real one has six arms. Folding in three is the trick.
flow.kid: Fold the square into a triangle. Fold it in half. Now fold it into three, like a fan. Cut the top straight.
flow.context: This activity makes a paper snowflake with six arms, like a real one.

flow.do: Cut small notches and curves from both long edges. Don't cut all the way across.
flow.say: Cut little shapes from both edges. Every cut you make will appear six times. Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: Cut small shapes from both edges. Don't cut right across.

flow.do: Open it gently. Count the arms and look for matching cuts.
flow.say: Open it up. How many arms? Does every arm have the same cuts?
flow.kid: Open it slowly. Count the arms. Do they all match?

check.q: Why does every cut appear on all six arms of the paper snowflake?
options: The scissors cut six times by magic
All the layers were stacked together, so one cut went through every layer at once
Paper is made of hexagons
check.why: The paper was folded into twelve stacked layers, so one cut went through all of them. Half of the layers are flipped, so each arm is also a mirror image down its middle. A real snowflake is similar in one way: all six arms meet the same air at the same moment, so each change in the air shapes all six arms together.

activities.title: The Blot Butterfly: is a real butterfly this exact?

materials.item: a sheet of paper
poster paint or thick watercolour, two or three colours
a picture of a real butterfly, or a butterfly seen on a balcony plant

schedule.what: Paint on half a folded sheet, press, open and compare with a real butterfly.

activities.record: Stick in your blot butterfly. Write one way your painting is like a real butterfly and one way the two differ.

setup.art: A sheet folded in half and opened, with blobs of paint on one side of the fold.
setup.caption: 1. Drop paint on one side of the fold.

setup.art: Hands pressing the folded sheet flat, then opening it to show a matching butterfly pattern.
setup.caption: 2. Fold, press and open.

flow.do: 1. Fold the paper in half and open it. 2. Put blobs of paint on one side only, close to the fold. 3. Fold it shut and press firmly from the fold outwards. 4. Open it.
flow.say: Paint on one side only. When we fold and press, what will happen on the other side?
flow.kid: Fold the paper and open it. Put paint on one side. Fold and press hard. Open it.
flow.context: This activity makes a painted butterfly with a line of symmetry, then compares the painting with a real one.

flow.do: Find the line of symmetry. Then look closely at the real butterfly or the picture of one.
flow.say: Where is the line of symmetry? Now look at a real butterfly. Do her two wings match as exactly as your painting?
flow.kid: Find the fold line. Now look at a real butterfly. Do her wings match exactly?

flow.do: Talk about why a butterfly needs matching wings.
flow.say: A butterfly flies by flapping both wings together. What would happen if one wing were much bigger?
flow.kid: A butterfly flaps both wings together. What if one wing were bigger?

ask.q: Why does a butterfly need two matching wings?
good: So she can fly straight.
If one wing pushed more air, she would fly in circles.

flow.parent: A butterfly has to fly straight to flowers and away from birds. Two matching wings push the same amount of air on each side. Real wings nearly match, but never exactly.

activities.title: My Two Halves: how even is my body?

materials.item: a ruler or a measuring tape
paper and pencil

schedule.what: Measure left and right hand spans and feet, and feel where the heart beats.

activities.record: Make a table with 'left' and 'right' for hand span and foot length.

setup.art: A child's hand spread wide on a ruler, measuring from thumb tip to little finger tip.
setup.caption: 1. Measure each hand span.

setup.art: A child drawing round both feet on a sheet of paper and measuring each outline.
setup.caption: 2. Draw round both feet and measure them.

flow.do: 1. Spread each hand on the ruler and measure from thumb tip to little finger tip. 2. Stand on paper, draw round each foot, and measure each outline from heel to big toe. 3. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Your body has a left half and a right half. Do they match exactly? Let's measure.
flow.kid: Measure your left hand span. Then your right. Draw round both feet. Measure them too.
flow.context: This activity checks how closely your own body's left and right halves match.
flow.parent: Differences of a millimetre or two may just be measuring error. A difference of a few millimetres or more is a real difference between your two sides.

flow.do: Put a hand flat on the middle of the chest, then a little to the left, and feel for the heartbeat.
flow.say: Let's feel for the heart. Is it in the middle, or more on one side?
flow.kid: Put your hand on your chest. Move it a little left. Can you feel your heart beat?
flow.parent: The heart sits behind the breastbone, tipped to the left, so the beat is usually easiest to feel a little left of the middle.

flow.do: Compare the numbers.
flow.say: Were the two sides exactly the same? Why might they be a little different?
flow.kid: Were your two sides the same? Close, or exact?

good: Nearly, but not exactly.
My hands were a few millimetres different.
My heart is on the left.

activities.title: The Window Plant: which way does symmetry break?

materials.item: a potted plant that has stood beside a window for at least two weeks, such as a money plant, tulsi or any balcony plant

schedule.what: Look at a window plant from above and from each side, and find which side has more leaves.

activities.record: Draw the plant from above. Draw an arrow towards the window.

setup.art: A potted tulsi on a windowsill, seen from above, with more leaves on the side facing the window.
setup.caption: 1. Look down on the plant from above.

setup.art: The same plant seen from the room side, leaning towards the glass.
setup.caption: 2. Look from the side. Which way does the plant lean?

flow.do: 1. Look down on the plant from above. 2. Count the leaves on the window side and the room side. 3. Look from the side to see if the stems lean.
flow.say: Is this plant the same on every side? Count the leaves on the window side and on the room side.
flow.kid: Look down on the plant. Count leaves on the window side. Count leaves on the room side.
flow.context: This activity looks for a place where a plant's symmetry breaks, and asks why.

flow.do: Talk about why the sides differ.
flow.say: A plant needs light to make food. What was different on the window side?
flow.kid: Plants make food with light. Which side got more light?

ask.q: Why is the plant not even on all sides?
good: The window side gets more light.
She grows towards the light to make more food.
Her two sides met different conditions.

flow.parent: Light came from one side only, so the plant grew more on that side and bent towards it. Turning the pot a quarter turn every few days helps her grow more evenly.

projects.title: A Week of Kolams

materials.item: rice flour or chalk, or a pencil and a notebook
a phone camera, if you have one, to photograph each kolam

schedule.what: Draw a kolam with one line of symmetry only.
Draw a kolam with order 2 rotational symmetry but no line of symmetry.
Draw a kolam with order 4 and four lines of symmetry.
Draw a kolam or rangoli with order 6 or 8, like a flower.
Lay all five drawings or photos side by side and label each one's symmetry.

projects.record: One page per day: the kolam, its lines of symmetry drawn in pencil, and its order of rotational symmetry.

setup.art: Five small kolams drawn in a notebook, each a little more complex, labelled Day 1 to Day 5.
setup.caption: 1. Draw one kolam each day, each with a different symmetry.

setup.art: The five kolams laid out side by side with their lines of symmetry drawn in red.
setup.caption: 2. On day 5, compare them all.

flow.do: Day 1: draw a pattern with one line of symmetry only, like a butterfly or a temple doorway.
flow.say: Today's kolam has just one fold line. What in nature has one fold line?
flow.kid: Draw a kolam with one fold line only. Like a butterfly.
flow.context: This is day 1 of A Week of Kolams. Each day you draw a pattern with a different kind of symmetry.
flow.parent: If you draw with rice flour indoors, sweep it up afterwards. No rice flour? Use a pencil and notebook.

flow.do: Day 2: draw a pattern that looks the same after half a turn but has no fold line, like the letter S.
flow.say: Today's kolam must match after half a turn, but must not fold to match. That's tricky. Try swirls.
flow.kid: Draw a kolam that matches after half a turn. It must not fold to match.

flow.do: Day 3: draw a kolam with four matching quarters and four fold lines.
flow.say: Draw one quarter, then turn and repeat. Make each quarter a mirror image of itself too, so the kolam also folds to match.
flow.kid: Draw four matching quarters. Make it fold four ways too.

flow.do: Day 4: draw a flower kolam or rangoli with 6 or 8 petals.
flow.say: Today, draw a flower. Will you give it 6 petals, like the 6 arms of a snowflake, or 8?
flow.kid: Draw a flower kolam with 6 or 8 petals.

flow.do: Day 5: lay out all five, and label each with its lines of symmetry and order.
flow.say: Which was hardest to draw? Which kind of symmetry do you see most often in nature?
flow.kid: Put all five kolams in a row. Label each one. Which was hardest?

ask.q: Which kolam is most like a flower, and which is most like your body?
good: The flower kolam is like a periwinkle, with rotational symmetry.
The day 1 kolam is like my body, with one fold line.

challenges.title: The Pinwheel Puzzle: why a spinner needs a twist
challenges.problem: Make a paper pinwheel that spins when you blow on it. Then find out what kind of symmetry it has, and why a pinwheel with a fold line would not spin.
constraints: Use one square of paper, a pin, and a pencil with an eraser or a straw.
It must spin when you blow on it from the front.
A grown-up pushes in the pin.
materials: a square of paper, about 15 cm on each side
a pencil with an eraser, or a stiff straw
general: Cut from each corner towards the centre, stopping halfway. Fold every other point into the centre and pin them through the middle into the eraser.
It has four blades, all bent the same way round, so the pinwheel looks the same after each quarter turn.
creative: Try 3 blades or 6 blades, cut from a triangle or hexagon of paper.
Bend two blades one way and two the other. Does it still spin?
Look at a ceiling fan while it is switched off. Are all its blades tilted the same way round?
challenges.your_turn: Design your own spinner, with any number of blades. Predict its order of rotational symmetry, then test whether it spins.

setup.art: A square of paper with four cuts from the corners towards the centre, and every other point folded to the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Cut, fold every other point to the centre and pin.

setup.art: A finished pinwheel on a pencil, spinning as a child blows on it.
setup.caption: 2. Blow on it. Then look for fold lines.

flow.do: 1. Cut from each corner towards the centre, stopping halfway. 2. Fold every other point to the middle. 3. A grown-up pins them through the centre into the eraser.
flow.say: Let's make a pinwheel. Fold every other point, all going the same way round.
flow.kid: Cut from each corner to halfway. Fold every other point to the middle. Ask a grown-up to pin it.
flow.context: This challenge makes a pinwheel and asks why a spinner needs rotational symmetry but no fold line.

flow.do: Blow on it. Then check its symmetry with the turn test and the fold test.
flow.say: It spins! How many times does it look the same in one turn? Can you find a fold line?
flow.kid: Blow on it. How many times does it match in one turn? Is there a fold line?

check.q: Your four-blade pinwheel looks the same after each quarter turn, but it has no fold line. Why does that help it spin?
options: All the blades are bent the same way round, so they all push the air the same way and turn the pinwheel one way
Paper spins better without fold lines
Pins only work with no fold lines
check.why: Every blade is tilted the same way round, so each one turns the pinwheel in the same direction. If it had a fold line, half the blades would be bent the other way and push it the other way, so the pushes would cancel out.

flow.do: Make a second pinwheel with two blades bent the wrong way. Compare.
flow.say: Now let's test the idea. Bend two blades the other way. What happens?
flow.kid: Make one with two blades bent the other way. Does it spin?
flow.parent: Expect it to spin badly or not at all, because the pushes partly cancel. If it still turns a little, that is because the pushes do not cancel perfectly.

challenges.safety: A pin is sharp. A grown-up pushes it in and presses the tip into the eraser.

challenges.title: Tile the Floor: which shape covers it with no gaps?
challenges.problem: Bees store honey and raise their young in wax cells. Making wax costs a bee a lot of food, so the best cells have no gaps. Find which shapes fit together with no gaps, and then find out which of them is best for a bee.
constraints: Make each kind of shape the same size, by tracing a template.
Lay the shapes edge to edge on a table, with no gaps and no overlaps, to test each kind.
materials: old card, such as a cereal box
a bottle cap, about 3 cm across, to draw circles
general: Squares and equal-sided triangles cover a floor with no gaps.
Hexagons cover it with no gaps too.
creative: Count how many shapes meet at one corner of your patch: 3 hexagons, 4 squares or 6 triangles. Why can circles never fit?
Look at floor tiles in your building. Which shapes do people use?
Try pentagons, five-sided shapes. Do they fit without gaps?
challenges.your_turn: Design your own tile shape that covers a floor with no gaps. It doesn't have to be regular. Test it.

setup.art: Card circles, squares, triangles and hexagons laid out edge to edge, with gaps between the circles.
setup.caption: 1. Make a template of each shape and cut 6 of each.

setup.art: A patch of card hexagons laid edge to edge on a table with no gaps.
setup.caption: 2. Lay each kind edge to edge. Which ones leave gaps?

flow.do: 1. Trace around the bottle cap on card and cut out 6 circles. 2. Measure across your circle and halve it. Cut a paper strip that long. 3. Start anywhere on the edge of a traced circle and mark the strip's length round the edge, six times. The six marks are the corners of a hexagon: join them, cut it out and use it as a template. 4. Join every second mark instead to get an equal-sided triangle, and cut that out as a template too. 5. Draw a square with sides about 2 cm. 6. Trace and cut so you have 6 of each shape.
flow.say: A bee needs cells with no gaps, using as little wax as she can. Let's make circles, squares, triangles and hexagons and test which ones fit together.
flow.kid: Trace the bottle cap for circles. Use the paper strip to find the six corners of a hexagon. Join every second corner for a triangle. Draw a square. Cut 6 of each.
flow.context: This challenge is about why honeycomb cells are hexagons. It starts with the bee's own problem: making wax costs her a lot of food.

flow.do: Lay each kind of shape edge to edge in turn.
flow.say: Which shapes leave gaps? Which fit together perfectly?
flow.kid: Lay each kind edge to edge. Which ones leave gaps?

flow.do: Talk about which is best for a bee.
flow.say: Squares, triangles and hexagons all fit. Mathematicians have proved that hexagons use the least wall for the space inside. Why does that matter to a bee?
flow.kid: Hexagons need the least wall. Why is that good for a bee?

check.q: Why is a hexagon the best shape for honeycomb?
options: It leaves no gaps and needs the least wax wall for the honey it holds
Bees can only count to six
Hexagons are the prettiest
check.why: Hexagons fit together with no gaps, and of all the shapes that do, they use the least wall for the space they hold. Thomas Hales proved this in 1999. So a bee saves wax, and the food that wax costs her. Circles leave gaps, which waste space.

challenges.safety: Cut with the scissors pointing away from your fingers. Children under 8 cut with a grown-up beside them.
