quiz.p: You fold a picture of a butterfly down the middle, and the two halves match exactly. What is the fold called?
quiz.why: The fold that splits a shape into two matching halves is a line of symmetry, also called a mirror line. 'Centre' is the point a shape turns around, which is for rotational symmetry.

quiz.p: A ceiling fan has three blades. With the fan switched off, you turn it slowly. How many times does it look exactly the same in one full turn?
quiz.why: It looks the same after each third of a turn, so 3 times. That is order 3 rotational symmetry. If you picked 6, you counted the gaps as well as the blades.

quiz.p: Which of these has rotational symmetry but no line of symmetry?
quiz.why: The letter S looks the same after half a turn, but no fold makes its halves match. The letter A and a butterfly have a line of symmetry but no rotational symmetry. A square has both.

quiz.p: You make a raft of same-sized soap bubbles and cover it with a clear lid. What shape are most of the bubbles in the middle?
quiz.why: Each bubble in the middle is pressed equally by about six neighbours, and the walls meet three at a time at equal angles. So most become six-sided. If you guessed squares, try it: four walls meeting at a point slide apart into threes.

quiz.p: In a bubble raft, why are the bubbles at the edge lopsided?
opts: They are pressed by bubbles on one side only
The soap is thinner at the edge
quiz.why: An edge bubble has neighbours on one side and open water or the plate on the other. The push is not the same all round, so the shape is not even. The middle bubbles have the same push from every side.

quiz.p: Why does a snowflake have six arms?
opts: In ice, water molecules join in rings of six
Snowflakes are cut by the wind
quiz.why: Water molecules join in six-sided rings when they freeze, so ice crystals grow in six directions. The arms match because they grow in the same air at the same time.

quiz.p: A snowflake's six arms usually match closely. What is the best reason?
opts: Each arm copies the others by touching them
All six arms grow in the same air at the same moments
quiz.why: A snowflake is tiny, so each change in the air reaches all six arms together. When one arm grows a branch, the others grow the same branch at the same time. The arms do not touch or copy each other.

quiz.p: A plant needs bees to carry her pollen. How does a flower with even petals all round help her?
opts: Bees can find her and land from any side
Even petals keep the rain off
quiz.why: A round, even flower is easy for a bee to spot and can be visited from any direction. Experiments show many bees prefer symmetrical patterns. The plant gains because the bee carries her pollen to the next flower.

quiz.p: A tulsi flower has one line of symmetry and a lip at the bottom. How does this help the plant?
opts: Bees land on the lip the same way up every time, so pollen touches the same place on each bee
quiz.why: A bee always lands on the lip the right way up. So the pollen is put on the same part of her body each time, and touches the next flower in the right place.

quiz.p: Why do fish, ants and people have a left side and a right side that nearly match?
opts: They move forward, so they meet the world front first and their two sides meet it in the same way
quiz.why: Animals that move forward have their mouth and eyes at the front, and their left and right sides meet the world in the same way. Animals that drift, like jellyfish, are often the same all the way round.

quiz.p: A kolam is made by drawing one quarter, then turning and drawing the same quarter three more times. What order of rotational symmetry does it have?
quiz.why: Four matching quarters, each a quarter turn apart, make the kolam look the same 4 times in one full turn.

quiz.p: A money plant beside a window has more leaves on the window side. What does this break in her symmetry tell you?
opts: The window side got more light
Plants always grow on one side
quiz.why: A break in symmetry is a clue that one side met something different. Here, light came from the window, and the plant grew more leaves where she could make more food.

items.p: Sort these things by the fold test. Does each one have a line of symmetry?
items.a: see items
items.why: A shape has a line of symmetry if a fold makes its halves match. The letters S and Z only match when turned, not folded. A hand has no fold that matches. A strong answer imagines the fold for each one.

items.p: You stick a bindi on the edge of a picture of a five-petalled periwinkle flower and turn the picture slowly. How many times does it look the same in one full turn?
items.why: Each of the five petals takes the place of the next one after one-fifth of a turn. So it matches 5 times, which is order 5.

items.p: 'Every shape looks the same after one full turn.' Is this true?
items.why: True. After a full turn, everything is back where it started. That is why a shape that only matches at the full turn has order 1, which means no rotational symmetry.

items.p: A flat shape with six straight sides is called a ____.
items.why: Hexagon means six-sided. Honeycomb cells and the squashed bubbles in the middle of a bubble raft are hexagons.

items.p: A butterfly's left wing and right wing match when you fold along her line of ____.
items.why: The fold line that makes the two halves match is the line of symmetry. A butterfly has one.

items.p: How many lines of symmetry does a square floor tile have?
items.why: A square can be folded along two lines through the middles of opposite sides and along two diagonals. That makes 4.

items.p: Look at the drawing of a bubble raft. Count the walls of the bubble marked with a star in the middle.
items.why: Bubbles in the middle of a raft of same-sized bubbles usually have 6 walls. A strong answer touches each wall once while counting, so none is counted twice.
items.art: A bubble raft drawn from above, with neat hexagonal cells in the middle, one marked with a star, and lopsided cells at the edge.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: a fold line where two halves match
looks the same when turned part of the way round
how many times a shape matches in one full turn
an animal that carries pollen between flowers
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These words come up all through the unit. A strong answer could also give an example of each, such as a periwinkle for order 5.

items.p: Which of these has bilateral symmetry, a left half and a right half that match?
items.why: Your body has one line of symmetry, from head to feet. A fan, a snowflake and a jellyfish all have rotational symmetry around a centre.

items.p: A bhindi is cut across its middle. It shows 5 rows of seeds around the centre. What order of rotational symmetry does the cut face have?
items.why: Five repeating seed rows around the centre give order 5. It matches itself 5 times in one full turn.

items.p: A butterfly needs two matching wings. What is the main reason?
opts: So both wings push the same amount of air and she flies straight
So she can fold them into a box
items.why: When both wings push the same amount of air, she flies straight to flowers and away from birds. A butterfly with one big wing would turn in circles.

items.p: In your bubble raft, the middle bubbles and the edge bubbles were made of the same soap, under the same lid. Why were they different shapes?
items.a: The middle bubbles were pressed equally on every side by bubbles of the same size, so they became even, six-sided cells. The edge bubbles had bubbles on one side only and open water or the plate on the other. The push was not even, so they were lopsided.
items.why: A strong answer names what was the same (soap, lid, size) and what was different (the push around each bubble), and links the difference to the shape.

items.p: Draw a shape that has exactly one line of symmetry and no rotational symmetry. Then draw a shape that has rotational symmetry but no line of symmetry.
items.a: For example, a butterfly or a heart for the first, and the letter S, the letter Z or a pinwheel for the second.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the dotted fold line on the first shape. For the second, it shows how the shape matches itself after a turn but no fold makes the halves match.

items.p: Two friends in Kochi look at a pot of periwinkle flowers. Each flower has five matching petals.

views.says: The flowers are even because bees like even flowers best. Bees chose them.
The flowers are even because the petals grow in a ring round the middle of the bud. That makes them even by themselves.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with more? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer sees that both can be part of the answer. Sneha is right that petals grow in a ring round the tip of the bud, which spaces them evenly. Anjali is right that experiments show bees learn and often prefer symmetrical patterns, and bees visiting more often may have helped such flowers spread over a long time. A strong answer says which matters more is still being studied.
items.why: Scientists agree on Sneha's point. Anjali's point is supported by bee experiments, but nobody yet knows how strong the effect is. Either side, argued with a reason, is a good answer.

items.p: A friend says a circle is the most symmetrical shape of all. Why might she be right?
items.a: A circle looks the same however little you turn it, and every line through its centre is a line of symmetry.
items.why: A strong answer says a circle matches itself after any turn and has endless lines of symmetry, unlike a square, which matches only after quarter turns.

items.p: A starfish has five arms. How many times does she look the same in one full turn?
items.why: Five matching arms around a centre give order 5. Interestingly, young starfish swim as two-sided larvae before they grow their five arms.

items.p: Three of these have rotational symmetry of order 6. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: A periwinkle has five petals, so order 5. A snowflake, a honeycomb cell and a hexagonal nut all have six matching parts.

items.p: A star fruit slice has order 5. How many lines of symmetry does it have?
items.why: A shape with 5 equal points has 5 lines of symmetry, each through one point and the middle of the gap opposite. A strong answer draws the lines to check.

items.p: Put the steps of the bubble raft experiment in order.
items: Lay a clear lid gently on top
Mix dishwashing liquid, sugar and water and pour the soapy water into a plate
Count the walls of 5 middle and 5 edge bubbles
Blow gently through a straw to make same-sized bubbles
a: Mix dishwashing liquid, sugar and water and pour the soapy water into a plate
Blow gently through a straw to make same-sized bubbles
Lay a clear lid gently on top
Count the walls of 5 middle and 5 edge bubbles
items.why: First make the soapy layer, then the bubbles, then flatten them, then count. Counting both middle and edge bubbles lets you compare.

items.p: In a raft of soap bubbles, one bubble in the middle is much smaller than its neighbours. How many walls is it most likely to have?
items.why: Smaller bubbles in a foam tend to have fewer walls, and bigger ones more. Only bubbles of the same size, pressed equally, come out as six-sided hexagons.

items.p: 'Every real snowflake is perfectly symmetrical.' Is this true?
items.why: False. Most real snowflakes are a little uneven, broken or stuck to others. The perfect ones in books were picked out by photographers. A strong answer says why some are uneven: one side met slightly different air, or the snowflake bumped into something.

items.p: A scientist grows snowflakes in a cold laboratory. What could he change to make them grow as a plate, a needle or a branching star?
opts: The temperature and the moisture of the air
items.why: Temperature and moisture decide the shape. That is why a snowflake's arms change as it falls through different air, and why all six arms change together.

items.p: A jellyfish drifts in the sea. Food and danger can reach her from any side, so her body is the same all the way round. This is called ____ symmetry.
items.why: Radial symmetry is symmetry all the way round a centre, like spokes on a wheel. Animals that move forward instead have bilateral symmetry.

items.p: Label the drawing of a periwinkle flower: draw one line of symmetry, mark the centre, and write its order of rotational symmetry.
items.a: A line from the tip of one petal through the centre to the gap between the opposite petals, a dot at the centre, and 'order 5'.
items.why: A five-petalled flower has 5 lines of symmetry, each through one petal tip and the centre. Its order is 5. A strong answer draws the line through a petal tip on one side and through the gap between two petals on the other.
items.art: A large drawing of a five-petalled periwinkle flower.

items.p: A plant cannot walk to another plant to share her pollen. Explain how a symmetrical flower helps her solve this problem.
items.a: She needs a bee or another pollinator to carry the pollen. A symmetrical flower is easy for a bee to spot and land on. Many bees prefer symmetrical flowers. A flower with a landing lip lets the bee land the same way every time, so the pollen goes onto the same part of the bee's body and reaches the next flower.
items.why: A strong answer starts with the plant's problem, then says how the shape helps the bee find or land, and so carry pollen.

items.p: Many people think an even shape must be planned by someone. Use what you saw in this unit to argue against this.
items.a: In the bubble raft, nobody drew the hexagons. The bubbles became six-sided because each was pressed equally on every side. A snowflake grows six matching arms with no plan, because all six arms grow in the same air at the same time.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence from the bubble raft or the snowflake, not just an opinion.

items.p: A tree grows at the edge of a busy road, next to a tall building. Predict what shape the tree will be, and explain why.
items.a: It will be lopsided, with more branches on the open side away from the building. The building blocks the light on one side, so the tree grows more where the light is.
items.why: A strong answer links the break in symmetry to one side meeting different conditions, like the window plant and the edge bubbles.

items.p: Draw a fish from the side and from above. On the view from above, draw her line of symmetry.
items.a: A fish from above with a line running from her mouth to her tail.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the fish's left and right halves match, and that the line runs from the front, where she meets the world first, to the back.
items.art: Two empty boxes labelled 'from the side' and 'from above'.

items.p: 'A rectangle that is not a square has four lines of symmetry.' Is this true?
items.why: False. A rectangle has two lines of symmetry, one across the middle each way, and order 2 rotational symmetry. Only a square has four lines. A strong answer thinks of folding a long, thin rectangle from corner to corner, and sees that the two halves do not match.

items.p: Three people talk about why honeycomb cells are hexagons.

views.says: Bees build hexagons because hexagons hold the most honey for the least wax. Wax costs a bee a lot of food.
Soft, warm wax pulls itself into hexagons, the way bubbles do. The bees don't have to plan it.
Bees shape their cells carefully, measuring them with their bodies. The hexagons are their work.

items.ask: Which view do you find most convincing? Use what you learned about bubbles and about the bees' problem. Then say what the other two have right.
items.a: A strong answer uses evidence: bubbles show that pressing and pulling can make hexagons without a plan, and hexagons really do use the least wall. It also gives the bees credit: scientists still argue how much the bees shape the cells and how much the wax does, and recent studies suggest bees build the walls directly. A strong answer says this is still argued.
items.why: This is a real debate among scientists. There is no single settled answer, so a good answer argues with evidence and admits what is unknown.

items.p: Which capital letter has both a line of symmetry and order 2 rotational symmetry?
items.why: H matches when folded across the middle or down the middle, and it looks the same after half a turn. A has only a fold line, S only a turn, and F neither.

items.p: A shape has 4 lines of symmetry. What is the smallest order of rotational symmetry it can have?
items.why: A flat shape with 4 lines of symmetry, like a square, also matches itself 4 times in one turn. Flipping a shape over one mirror line and then over another is the same as turning it. So a shape with several mirror lines always has rotational symmetry too.

items.p: You fold a paper square into 8 layers and cut a snowflake. How many arms will it have?
items.why: Folding into 8 gives a four-fold or eight-fold pattern, not six. A real snowflake has six arms. To get six, you fold the paper into three after the first two folds.

items.p: A snowflake falls past a warm chimney, so one side meets warmer air than the other. What will its arms most likely look like?
opts: The arms on the warm side grow differently from the others
items.why: The arms match only when they all meet the same air. If one side meets different air, those arms grow differently and the symmetry breaks. The break shows where the air was different.

items.p: A bubble raft sits right next to a ruler lying in the plate. What will the bubbles touching the ruler look like?
opts: Flat on the side touching the ruler
items.why: The ruler presses on one side only, so the walls touching it are straight and the bubbles are lopsided, like the edge bubbles at the rim of the plate. Wherever the push changes, the shape changes.

items.p: Sort these living things by their symmetry.
items.a: see items
items.why: Animals that move forward, like a crow and an earthworm, are bilateral. A tulsi flower is bilateral too, with a landing lip. A jellyfish, a sea anemone and a hibiscus flower are the same all the way round.

items.p: A snowflake has six arms. Each arm grows 4 side branches on each side. How many side branches does the whole snowflake have?
items.why: Each arm has 4 + 4 = 8 branches. Six arms have 6 × 8 = 48. A strong answer shows the working: branches per arm first, then times six.

items.p: 'If a shape has rotational symmetry, it must also have a line of symmetry.' Is this true?
items.why: False. A pinwheel and the letter S have rotational symmetry but no line of symmetry. A strong answer gives an example like these.

items.p: Your heart sits a little to the left. Your body has a left and a right side that nearly match. Why do you think the outside of your body is more even than the inside?
items.a: The outside meets the world, and moving forward means both sides meet the world in the same way, so it is useful for them to match. Inside, organs like the heart, stomach and liver can be packed in any way that fits, so they are not in matching pairs.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A strong answer links the evenness of the outside to how the body moves and meets the world, and says the inside has a different job.

items.p: The bubbles at the edge of the bubble raft are lopsided. A plant beside a window has more leaves on the window side. Explain how the two are alike.
items.a: Both break their symmetry because one side met something different. The edge bubbles were pressed on one side only. The plant got light on one side only. In both, the uneven shape shows which side was different.
items.why: A strong answer names the different condition in each case and says how the shape shows it.

items.p: In 1611, the astronomer Johannes Kepler wondered why every snowflake has six corners. If you could talk to him, what would you tell him, and how do scientists know?
items.a: I would tell him that in ice, water molecules join in rings of six, so ice grows in six directions, and the arms match because they grow in the same air together. Scientists know this from shining X-rays through ice to see where the molecules sit, and from Nakaya's snowflakes grown in a laboratory.
items.why: A strong answer gives both parts: why six, and why the arms match, and names how we know.

items.p: An engineer builds a fan whose blades are bent half one way and half the other. Predict what happens when it is switched on, and explain.
items.a: It will hardly turn. The blades bent one way push the fan one way, and the blades bent the other way push it the other way. The pushes cancel out.
items.why: A strong answer uses the pinwheel challenge: a spinner needs rotational symmetry without a line of symmetry.

items.p: Design a tile that can cover a floor with no gaps, and draw how 6 of them fit together.
items.a: Any shape that fits without gaps: a square, an equal-sided triangle, a hexagon, or a cleverer shape.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the tiles meeting edge to edge with no gaps or overlaps. Extra credit for a shape that is not a square, triangle or hexagon.

items.p: Two cousins, Meenakshi and Arjun, argue about whether symmetry is everywhere in nature.

views.says: Nature loves symmetry. Look at flowers, snowflakes and our faces.
Nature is never really symmetrical. Every leaf and face is a bit lopsided.

items.ask: Who is more right? Use at least two examples you have seen, such as bubbles, flowers, leaves or your own hands. Then say what the other cousin has right.
items.a: A strong answer sees that both are partly right. Many natural shapes are nearly symmetrical, like bubbles in the middle of a raft, a snowflake's arms and a periwinkle. But none is perfectly even: bubbles at the edge, a plant leaning to a window and your own two hands show small breaks, each caused by something different on one side.
items.why: This question has no single right side. A strong answer uses evidence for both.

items.p: Three people say why so many people around the world make symmetrical art, from kolams to mandalas.

views.who: A grandmother who draws a kolam every morning in Madurai
views.says: We learned it from nature. Flowers and stars are even, so we draw them that way.
Our eyes and brains find symmetrical shapes easier to see and remember, so we enjoy them.
Symmetry is practical. When you make one part and repeat it, the work is quicker and stronger.

items.ask: Which reason do you find most convincing? Give your reason. Then say what one of the other two has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one and supports it, for example with how a kolam is drawn quarter by quarter (practical), or how quickly the eye spots a symmetrical pattern (perception), and gives credit to another view. Many people think all three play a part.
items.why: This is an open question. Any side argued with a reason, and fair to another view, is a good answer.

applications: Engineers make fan blades, propellers and wheels with rotational symmetry so they spin smoothly without wobbling.
Builders use symmetry in temples, gopurams, bridges and buildings so the weight is spread evenly.
Textile designers use mirror and turn symmetry in saree borders, block prints and carpets.
Scientists who study crystals use symmetry to work out how atoms and molecules are arranged, and to design medicines.
Honeycomb-shaped panels, made of hexagonal cells, are used in aircraft and packaging because they are light and strong.

open_questions.q: How much did bees choosing symmetrical flowers shape the flowers we see today?
open_questions.why_open: Bees learn and often prefer symmetrical patterns, but it is hard to measure how strongly this has shaped flowers over millions of years.

open_questions.q: How exactly do bees build hexagonal cells?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think warm wax pulls itself into hexagons. Others have filmed bees building hexagonal walls directly. The question is still argued.

open_questions.q: Why are living bodies nearly symmetrical, but uneven in the same few ways, such as the heart sitting on the left?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know some of the signals in a growing embryo that tell left from right, but not the whole story of how the first difference starts.

open_questions.q: Why do people find symmetry beautiful?
open_questions.why_open: Some say symmetry is a sign of health. Others say symmetrical shapes are easier to see, or that we are used to them from nature. Studies disagree, and it may be a mix.

maths.problem: In a bubble raft, the walls of 5 middle bubbles were counted: 6, 6, 5, 6, 7. How many walls is that altogether, and what is the usual number per bubble?
maths.answer: 30 walls altogether. 30 shared out among 5 bubbles is 6 each.
maths.explain: Add them: 6 + 6 + 5 + 6 + 7 = 30. Sharing 30 equally among 5 bubbles gives 6 each. The 5 and the 7 balance out: one is one less than 6, the other one more.
maths.context: This is about the bubble raft experiment, where you count the walls of crowded soap bubbles.
maths.why_maths: One bubble can be odd. Adding and sharing equally shows the usual number for a middle bubble.

maths.problem: A pulli kolam has 5 rows of 5 dots. Another has 7 rows of 7 dots. How many more dots does the bigger kolam have?
maths.explain: 5 rows of 5 is 25 dots. 7 rows of 7 is 49 dots. 49 take away 25 is 24.
maths.context: This is about drawing a pulli kolam, which starts with a square grid of dots.
maths.why_maths: Counting dots in rows and columns is multiplication. It tells you how much bigger a kolam will be before you start.

maths.problem: A paper snowflake has 6 arms. You cut 3 notches on each side of each arm. How many notches are there on the opened snowflake?
maths.explain: Each arm has 3 + 3 = 6 notches. 6 arms with 6 notches each is 6 × 6 = 36.
maths.context: This is about cutting a paper snowflake with six arms.
maths.why_maths: A symmetrical shape is many equal groups. Multiplying is a quick way to count all the repeated parts.

maths.problem: A kolam with order 4 rotational symmetry is drawn quarter by quarter. Each quarter takes 3 minutes. How long does the whole kolam take? What fraction is done after 2 quarters?
maths.answer: 12 minutes. After 2 quarters, half is done.
maths.explain: 4 quarters of 3 minutes is 4 × 3 = 12 minutes. 2 quarters out of 4 is the same as one half.
maths.context: This is about drawing a kolam one quarter at a time.
maths.why_maths: Each quarter of a symmetrical kolam is the same, so one quarter tells you about the whole.

maths.problem: Four lemons had 9, 11, 10 and 10 segments. Four bhindis had 5, 5, 5 and 5 seed rows. Which fruit's count varied more? What is the difference between the biggest and smallest lemon count?
maths.answer: The lemon varied more. The difference is 2.
maths.explain: The bhindi counts were all 5, so they did not vary. The lemon counts went from 9 to 11. 11 take away 9 is 2.
maths.context: This is about cutting fruits across and counting the parts around the centre.
maths.why_maths: Finding the biggest and smallest number shows at a glance whether a kind of fruit always repeats the same number of times.

roots.context: We have found symmetry in flowers, snowflakes, bubbles and kolams, and seen even shapes appear with no one drawing them. Now we ask what symmetry tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the bubble raft experiment, each bubble in the middle was pressed equally from every side. Most came out six-sided, like their neighbours. At the edge, bubbles were pressed on some sides only, and came out lopsided. Nobody drew the hexagons: an even push all round made an even shape.
deep_truth.habit: We think a neat, even shape needs a maker who plans it, the way a person plans a kolam. The bubble raft shows an even shape can also come from even conditions all round, and that an uneven shape points to the side where something was different.
deep_truth.evidence: In the bubble raft, the middle bubbles and the edge bubbles were the same soap, the same size and under the same lid. Only the push around them differed. The middle ones came out six-sided, and the edge ones came out lopsided.

three.who_am_i: You have a left side and a right side that nearly match, because you move forward and meet the world front first. Your heart sits a little to the left, so you are not perfectly even.
three.what_is_life: A flower's even petals help her bees find her and land on her. Her shape is part of how she lives with the bees.
three.what_is_this_world: Bubbles, snowflakes and crystals make even shapes with no plan drawn, because the same rules act the same way on every side.

roots.thread: A snowflake begins as one tiny piece of ice, the same on every side. One rule, water molecules joining in rings of six, acts the same way in all six directions, and six matching arms grow out. A kolam grows the same way: one quarter, turned and repeated, becomes the whole. Where the parts of a shape differ, something outside it was different.

teachings.source: Avatamsaka Sutra, the image of Indra's net
teachings.teaching: Indra's net has a jewel at every knot. Each jewel reflects every other jewel, so each one holds the whole net.
teachings.link: In a bubble raft, each bubble's shape is made by the bubbles pressing around it, and it presses on them in turn. No bubble is shaped on its own.

teachings.source: Plato, Timaeus (the passage on the five regular solids)
teachings.teaching: Plato taught that fire, air, water and earth are made of tiny perfectly regular shapes, such as cubes and pyramids.
teachings.link: Plato's shapes were wrong. But he was right that the smallest parts of matter sit in regular patterns: in ice, water molecules really do join in rings of six.

science.text: Soap films meet three at a time at equal angles, which is why same-sized bubbles pressed together become hexagons. Joseph Plateau set out the rules in 1873.

In 1918, the mathematician Emmy Noether proved that each symmetry in the laws of physics comes with something whose total amount never changes. For example, the laws are the same at every moment, and that is why energy is never made or lost.

other_view.view: In living things, symmetry comes mostly from genes and from what helped their ancestors survive, not only from even conditions. A flower's five petals come out even when the wind blows on her from one side too, because her bud grows that way.

practice.title: Even breath
practice.say: Let's sit tall and put one hand on each side of our ribs. Breathe in slowly. Do both hands rise together? Breathe out slowly. Now move one hand a little left of the middle of your chest. Can you feel your heart beating there? Our two sides breathe together, but our heart sits on one side. Take three more slow breaths and feel both.
practice.kid: Sit tall. Put a hand on each side of your ribs. Breathe in slowly. Do both hands rise together? Now feel your heart. It is a little to the left. Breathe slowly three more times.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home in a city flat, with the materials listed. The bubble raft uses a rimmed steel plate, a cup of water, a tablespoon of dishwashing liquid, a little sugar, a straw and a clear takeaway lid. A layer of soapy water a few millimetres deep lets the straw tip sit under the surface, and gentle blowing gives same-sized bubbles. The bubbles are low domes, so the six-sided shape is clear but not perfect; without a lid, children count neighbours instead. The fruit experiment uses bhindi, lemons, cucumbers and tomatoes from the kitchen, cut by a grown-up. The paper snowflake is folded into twelve layers for six arms. The challenge to tile a floor makes its own circle, square, triangle and hexagon templates from a bottle cap and a paper strip. The kolam can be drawn with rice flour at the door or with a pencil on paper. The window plant activity needs a potted plant that has stood by a window for two weeks. The spine fits about 80 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1555, a Swedish writer, Olaus Magnus, printed the first known pictures of snowflakes in Europe. Most of his snowflakes were odd shapes, such as a bell, a hand and an arrow. People did not yet look closely enough to see that snowflakes have six arms. In 1611, the astronomer Johannes Kepler noticed that every snowflake he saw had six corners. He wrote a little book about it as a New Year's gift for a friend, and asked why. He guessed that it had to do with how tiny pieces of matter pack together, but he could not prove it. In 1665, Robert Hooke looked at snowflakes through a microscope and drew their six arms in detail. In 1885, Wilson Bentley, a farmer in America, took the first photographs of single snowflakes. In the 1930s, Ukichiro Nakaya in Japan grew snowflakes in a cold room and showed how the air shapes their arms. Later, scientists shone X-rays through ice and found that water molecules join in rings of six. Kepler's guess about packing had been close.
how_we_found_out.who: Olaus Magnus, Johannes Kepler, Robert Hooke, Wilson Bentley and Ukichiro Nakaya
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: The first printed pictures showed snowflakes in many shapes, such as a bell, a hand and an arrow. Careful looking, first with the eye, then with a microscope and a camera, showed that snowflakes always grow six arms.
